newsitem.title: UK: Dlr ends mixed in Europe, shrugs off trade data.
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends mixed in Europe, shrugs off trade data.

text.p: The dollar closed little chagned against the mark but gained ground versus the yen as the Japanese unit suffered a fresh bout of weakness, dealers said.

Initial dollar sales after the release of higher-than- expected U.S. trade data were reversed as the dollar caught bids below 1.54 marks. The August trade gap fell 6.6 percent to $10.83 billion against $8.5 billion forecast.
A sharp rise in sterling/mark in late trade here also gave the dollar a helping hand, dealers said.
"The dollar recovered quickly after the data, and the sterling move added impetus," said Merita Bank's Alan Collins.
At 1501 GMT the dollar was at 1.5424/27 marks and 112.51/61 yen, compared with 1.5436/41 and 112.20/30 in late European trading on Thursday.

Sterling rose to 2.4568 marks, its highest since December 1994, on a newspaper report that a member of the UK Treasury's panel of independent economic advisor, Tim Congdon, said the UK should raise official interest rates by a full percentage point.
Congdon told the Evening Standard newspaper a rise of about one point from 5.75 percent at present would avert the need for more drastic moves at a later date.

Sterling also pushed higher against the dollar to a high of $1.5930, its highest since early October 1995. Dealers said cable was pushed higher amid talk that a large option with a knock-out strike at $1.59 expired today.
The holder of the option had actively tried to hold sterling below that level until the option expired, dealers said.
"That added to the sterling move higher," said Collins, who is head of technical analysis at Merita Bank.
The U.S. trade data proved to be a bit of a non-event as the underlying dollar tone remains firm, even though the unit might look for some consolidation now, dealers said.

"The trade data are mixed," said Jeremy Hawkins, chief economic advisor at Bank America in London. "The overall bottom line was larger than expected, with no significant revision to July data suggesting that net exports will act as a major drag on third quarter GPD."
However, the breakdown of the data was more positive, with both imports and exports rising and the bilateral short-fall with Japan narrowing 11.8 percent to $3.8 billion.
Analysts said dollar/yen had pushed to a fresh 33-month high at 112.63 yen earlier as dealers seemed eager to test the Bank of Japan's (BOJ) patience with a stronger dollar/yen.
"It looks as if there are some players who want to see how far the BOJ will allow the dollar to go higher before intervening again," said Tim Fox, treasury economist at Standard Chartered in London.

The more robust dollar/yen tone was by another sharp decline in the Japanese trade surplus, on a declining trend over the past year. It plunged by 30.3 percent in September year-on-year to 779.5 billion yen.
The Japanese elections are a risk factor but are not expected to bring major surprises for the forex market, dealers said.

The increased political uncertainty in Russia, highlighted by the sacking of security chief Alexander Lebed on Thursday, remained a positive backdrop for the dollar but analysts said the mark is unlikely to suffer further from the Russia factor.

While the idea that Germany is more exposed to Russia than any other western economy in geographical and trade terms still holds true, the exposure is far less significant now than it used to be, analysts said.
Moreover, compared to the early 1990s, Russia's relations with the west are on a much more multilateral basis.
-- Astrid Zweynert London newsroom + 44 171 542 7792
